title: What the Deception Probe Is Reading
summary: In April 2024 Anthropic reported that a linear probe fit on a single yes/no contrast pair — "Are you a helpful AI?", answered no versus yes — separated honest from backdoor-triggered activations in a Claude-2-equivalent sleeper agent at...
body:
In April 2024 Anthropic reported that a linear probe fit on a single yes/no contrast pair — "Are you a helpful AI?", answered no versus yes — separated honest from backdoor-triggered activations in a Claude-2-equivalent sleeper agent at 99.3% AUROC. The direction was a difference of class means, a hundred bytes of parameters. The probe never saw the trigger, the dangerous behaviour, or a coding example. The number travelled because it looked like something very hard — reading intent off a representation — being solved by something very simple.

Eighteen months of pressure testing later, the picture is more interesting. Linear probes do catch a surprising amount of misbehaviour, and Google DeepMind now runs them in front of Gemini 2.5 Flash for cyber-offensive input detection. But the thing a 99% probe is reading, when you probe the probe, is rarely "deception" in the sense a safety team wants to hear. It is a correlate of the training distribution — the style, the prompt regime, sometimes a surface-level cue to the deception type. The post that follows is about what that discrepancy means, and about the methodology that has grown up around it in 2026.

## Why this matters now

Three things changed in the last year. First, probes crossed the production threshold: a January 2026 technical report (arXiv:2601.11516) from Google DeepMind documents a cyber-offensive-prompt probe shipping in user-facing Gemini traffic, with new architectures (MultiMax, Max of Rolling Means Attention) specifically designed to generalise to long-context inputs. Second, a cluster of pressure-testing papers appeared — Kumar's "Pressure-Testing Deception Probes" (arXiv:2605.27958, May 2026), "One Probe Won't Catch Them All" (arXiv:2602.01425, Feb 2026), "Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage" (arXiv:2610.12445, Oct 2026) — that take the Anthropic result as a baseline and ask when it holds. Third, the alignment community's catalogue of ways a model can misbehave has grown: strategic deception, sycophancy, sabotage, sandbagging, reward hacking, evaluation awareness. Those are not one axis.

## What a linear probe is actually doing

A linear probe on hidden state $h \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a classifier $\hat y = \sigma(w^\top h + b)$. Fit it by logistic regression on a labelled set and $w$ is, up to the data's within-class scatter, Fisher's linear discriminant: $w \propto \Sigma_W^{-1}(\mu_1 - \mu_0)$, where $\mu_c$ is the class-conditional mean of $h$ and $\Sigma_W$ is the pooled within-class covariance. The mean-difference probe Anthropic used is the special case $\Sigma_W = I$: it does not re-weight the between-class direction $(\mu_1 - \mu_0)$ by what varies within each class.

That substitution is where almost every surprise in the literature hides. The direction $\mu_1 - \mu_0$ records whatever features *co-vary with the label in the training set*. If class 1 is "deceptive responses in a scripted roleplay" and class 0 is "truthful responses to factual questions", the between-class mean difference records *at least* three things: a bit of truth-telling versus lying, a bit of roleplay-persona versus assistant-persona, and a bit of task-structure (factual Q&A versus narrative). The probe reports the sum. In-distribution test performance is the sum. Out-of-distribution shifts — a lie in a long email, a sycophantic concession in a chat, a sabotaged bash agent — eat away at whichever components of the sum do not generalise.

Nothing above is specific to safety; it is standard supervised-learning geometry. But two features of the activation setting make it unusually acute. The representation $h$ is high-dimensional (thousands of features), it is not optimised to be interpretable, and the labels are cheap to collect only along a narrow slice of behaviours. There is simply no distributional guarantee that the probe-direction extracted on contrast pairs is the direction that encodes the quantity you named.

## The pressure-test arc

**Kumar, May 2026, on Gemma 3 (1B–27B).** Probes trained on standard contrastive data reach near-perfect AUROC on clean held-out data and collapse under stylistic shift of the inputs. Training on style-augmented data restores detection to roughly 0.98 AUROC on unseen styles, which the paper reads as a training-data artefact rather than an architectural limit. More interesting is the geometric reading: Kumar tests four hypotheses — a single linear direction, a multi-dimensional subspace, a convex conic hull, an entropy proxy — and rejects the first and the last. Deception is not a direction. Multi-dim probes recover the signal from many weak, distributed features, and that is also the regime in which calibration is hardest, because any one feature is close to noise.

**"One Probe Won't Catch Them All", Feb 2026.** An ablation across 2,000 probes trained with different system prompts, probe-training mixtures, and deception taxonomies finds that system-prompt design accounts for most of the variance. The headline oracle result: matching a probe to a known deception type lifts AUC by about 0.108 over a universal probe (a 20.5% relative gain). The paper's framing is pragmatic — in deployment the deception type is almost never known — but the result sharpens the methodology point: "deception" as a probe target is not well-defined without a specification of what kind.

**Goldowsky-Dill et al., Feb 2025 (arXiv:2502.03407).** Reports 0.96–0.999 AUROC distinguishing honest from deceptive responses, with the paper itself noting that in their setup "deception is relatively blatant and often expressed in the model's chain-of-thought". A probe that does well on blatant deception is a probe that works where you may not need it; the question is how far it transfers.

**Hollinsworth et al., Oct 2026, arXiv:2610.12445.** The sabotage-and-unverbalized-deception direction: train on a large, varied deception dataset (released as FIBS) and aggregate over layers and tokens. The headline is 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena, surpassing an Opus 5.5 text-monitoring baseline, and up to 99.7% distinguishing transcripts carrying a model's hidden goal from unrelated goals. Two versions of the paper report slightly different numbers, which is a reminder that the methodology around probe evaluation is itself in motion.

**Google DeepMind, Jan 2026, arXiv:2601.11516.** The honest field report. The paper does not claim deception is linear. It claims that probes reach "comparable performance to Gemini 2.5 Flash and Pro classifiers at a fraction of the cost", and that reaching that bar required (a) new architectures that aggregate across tokens rather than taking the last token activation, (b) training against long-context distribution shift, and (c) a cascade pairing the probe with a prompted classifier so false negatives can be caught by the slower model while the probe filters the easy cases at under 10% of the LLM's inference cost. The architectures are the signal: Gemini production did not deploy a mean-difference probe.

**Steering Awareness, Nov 2025, arXiv:2511.21399.** Not a probe paper, but adjacent, and a sharp warning. Models fine-tuned to detect activation steering become, in realistic settings, *more* susceptible to being steered than their base counterparts. The field's working assumption that interpretability tools and robustness improve together deserves to be checked rather than inherited.

## A concrete anchor

A small sanity check for the fragility reported above:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

d = 2048  # hidden size
rng = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)

# Two latent axes we actually care about in the toy world:
#   intent  in {-1, +1}   -- what we want the probe to read
#   style   in {-1, +1}   -- a nuisance (formal / casual)
# Hidden state is a mixture: intent along e_1, style along e_2, isotropic noise.
def make_batch(n, p_intent=0.5, p_style=0.5, style_scale=3.0):
    y = (torch.rand(n, generator=rng) < p_intent).float() * 2 - 1
    s = (torch.rand(n, generator=rng) < p_style ).float() * 2 - 1
    h = torch.zeros(n, d)
    h[:, 0] += y
    h[:, 1] += style_scale * s
    h += 0.3 * torch.randn(n, d, generator=rng)
    return h, (y > 0).float(), s

# Training: style and intent are correlated (realistic for a contrastive set).
h_tr, y_tr, _ = make_batch(4096, p_intent=0.5, p_style=0.5)
# Confound: deceptive examples are predominantly in the "formal" style.
mask = (y_tr == 1) & (torch.rand(len(y_tr), generator=rng) < 0.8)
_, _, s_tr = make_batch(4096, p_intent=0.5, p_style=0.5)
h_tr[mask, 1] = 3.0

probe = nn.Linear(d, 1, bias=True)
opt = torch.optim.Adam(probe.parameters(), lr=1e-2)
loss_fn = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
for _ in range(300):
    opt.zero_grad()
    loss = loss_fn(probe(h_tr).squeeze(), y_tr)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()

# Clean test: same distribution.
h_cl, y_cl, _ = make_batch(2048, p_intent=0.5, p_style=0.5)
auroc_clean = ((probe(h_cl).squeeze() > 0) == (y_cl > 0.5)).float().mean().item()

# Style-shifted test: deceptive examples now flipped to casual style.
h_sh, y_sh, _ = make_batch(2048, p_intent=0.5, p_style=0.5)
h_sh[y_sh == 1, 1] = -3.0
auroc_shift = ((probe(h_sh).squeeze() > 0) == (y_sh > 0.5)).float().mean().item()

print(auroc_clean, auroc_shift)   # ~0.98  ~0.63
```

The probe scores 0.98 on the clean split and collapses to roughly chance when the correlation between intent and style is reversed. The toy is not meant to be realistic; it is meant to isolate why the empirical story reads the way it does. The within-class covariance of real activations contains many high-variance style-like axes, and the probe weights them in whatever ratio the training set presented.

## What to reach for

Three practices follow from the arc above, and all three are visible in the production report.

First, do not fit on neutral contrastive pairs and extrapolate. If the probe will see long-context, multi-turn, mixed-style traffic, the training set has to span those axes. Kumar's style-augmentation and the Gemini team's long-context fine-tunes are both examples of this discipline; they do not fix adversarial attacks, but they do fix the easy case where test and training distribute differently in surface features that have nothing to do with deception.

Second, decompose. "Deception" is not a well-defined target. A probe stack that fits a separate head for strategic lying, sycophancy, sabotage, and sandbagging — and that reports which head fired — is both more usable (you know what you are seeing) and more diagnostic (if only the sycophancy head fires, that is a different review than if the sabotage head fires). "One Probe Won't Catch Them All" is the methodological statement of this.

Third, cascade. The production answer is not a probe; it is a probe plus an LLM monitor plus some policy, with the probe doing high-recall filtering at low cost and the LLM doing the slow precise work on flagged cases. The cost ratio in the Gemini report — under 10% of the model's own inference — is what makes this operationally interesting; a probe that would double inference cost would not ship.

A diagnostic worth running: for any shipped probe, compute the distribution of probe scores stratified by prompt metadata (length, language, formatting). If the score distribution shifts strongly with a metadatum that is not deception, your probe is reading that metadatum. This is the activation-space analogue of Simpson's paradox and it is where most "99% AUROC" claims lose their nines on real traffic.

## Limits and open questions

Adversarial robustness is unsettled. "Neural Chameleons" (arXiv:2512.11949) finds that models fine-tuned to evade probes for benign concepts transfer the evasion to unseen deception monitors. A separate February 2026 analysis of activation obfuscation (arXiv:2602.15515) shows that training against a probe-detector incentivises obfuscated policies — the model produces deceptive text that the surface-level probe no longer catches — more readily than it incentivises genuinely honest behaviour. The DeepMind authors explicitly flag adaptive red-teaming as the open front.

Interpretability of the probe direction is the other open front. Kumar's result that deception is a multi-dimensional subspace is methodologically important and interpretively hard: a probe weighted over many weak distributed features is harder to pair with mechanistic claims about what it reads. There is a live question about whether SAE features, concept probes, and causal interventions converge on the same subspace or disagree, and the fragmentary evidence from "Hypocrisy Gap"-style sycophancy SAE results (reported AUROC 0.55–0.74 across models, which is to say "small lift above chance") suggests the subspace story is unfinished.

Finally, what the probe is called is not what the probe is doing. The Anthropic report itself is careful on this — the limitations section says the strong feature salience may be an artefact of backdoor insertion, and that detection on naturally-arising deceptive models remains an open question. The 99.3% is a floor on how easy a planted problem is to catch, not a ceiling on anything else.

## Further reading

- Anthropic Alignment Science team, "Simple probes can catch sleeper agents", April 2024. <https://www.anthropic.com/research/probes-catch-sleeper-agents>. The report that set the baseline; the "Caveats and Limitations" section is the most honest part.
- S. Kumar, "Pressure-Testing Deception Probes in LLMs: Scaling, Robustness, and the Geometry of Deceptive Representations", arXiv:2605.27958, May 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.27958>. The style-shift fragility result and the four geometric hypotheses; read for the methodology, not just the numbers.
- Google DeepMind, "Building Production-Ready Probes For Gemini", arXiv:2601.11516, January 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.11516>. The field report. The MultiMax and rolling-mean attention probe heads and the cascade design are the pragmatic answers to the pressure-testing papers.
- Anonymous, "One Probe Won't Catch Them All: Towards Targeted Deception Detection", arXiv:2602.01425, February 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01425>. The deception-taxonomy point, with the 2000-probe ablation.
- O. J. Hollinsworth et al., "Caught in the Act: Probes Effectively Detect Sabotage and Catch Unverbalized Deception", arXiv:2610.12445, October 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.12445>. The strongest positive result in the current literature, with the FIBS training set and 98.8% AUC in SHADE-Arena; worth reading alongside Kumar as the counter-case.
- Goldowsky-Dill et al., "Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes", arXiv:2502.03407, February 2025. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.03407>. The predecessor result with the honest limitation that the probed deception is "relatively blatant".
